titulo: Sounds, alphabet and first words: Stress, the tilde, «tú» and «usted»

aula.objetivo: Spell in Spanish, read the letters that sound different from what you expect (j, g, c, z, qu, ll, ñ, rr, h), keep vowels full and clear, mark the stressed syllable, and say your first greetings, with «tú» and with «usted».

blocos.titulo: Stressed syllable, the accent mark, questions and forms of address
blocos.explicacao: Listen to «café», «hotel» and «teléfono»: each one has one stronger syllable. STEP 1: words ending in a vowel, «n» or «s» are stressed on the second-to-last syllable: «casa», «joven», «mesas». Words ending in another consonant are stressed on the last syllable: «hotel», «ciudad», «español». STEP 2: when a word breaks that rule, an accent mark (´) marks the stressed vowel: «café», «avión», «inglés», «fútbol», «teléfono». Spanish only uses the acute accent; there's no circumflex (^) and no diacritic merging like Portuguese's «crase». STEP 3: the accent mark also tells apart words that would otherwise look the same: «tú» (you) × «tu» (your), «él» (he) × «el» (the), «sí» (yes) × «si» (if). STEP 4: questions and exclamations open with ¿ and ¡ and close with ? and !: «¿Cómo estás?», «¡Hola!». Question words always carry an accent: «qué», «quién», «dónde», «cómo», «cuándo». STEP 5: with friends, family and younger people, use «tú» («¿Cómo estás?»). With strangers, older people and formal settings, use «usted», with the verb in the third person («¿Cómo está usted?»). In Colombia, for example, «usted» is even used within families; when in doubt, use «usted». STEP 6: for «you» (plural), Spain uses «vosotros» (informal) and «ustedes» (formal). In Latin America, «ustedes» is used for both. STEP 7: watch out for false friends, words that look familiar but mean something else; the table below has the first ones.
blocos.comparacao: English also uses an accent mark on some borrowed words, but Spanish has no circumflex and marks every question with an opening «¿», which English doesn't do. English «you» covers almost everyone; in Spanish the choice between «tú» and «usted» changes the verb form.

erros.motivo: It ends in a vowel, but the stress falls on the last syllable; that's why it carries an accent mark.
The stress falls on the third-to-last syllable; it always carries an accent mark.
The question word «cómo» carries an accent; without it, «como» means «I eat» or «like, as».
With strangers and older people, use «usted» and the verb in the third person.

blocos.titulo: Por la calle / On the street
blocos.contexto: Pablo greets Mr. Ruiz, using «usted», and then his friend Lucía, using «tú». Notice when the verb changes: «está» and «estás».

linhas.ru: — Buenos días, señor Ruiz. ¿Cómo está usted?
linhas.pt: — Good morning, Mr. Ruiz. How are you?
linhas.audio: Buenos días, señor Ruiz. ¿Cómo está usted?

linhas.pt: — Very well, thank you. And you?
— Fine, thank you. Bye, Mr. Ruiz.
— Very well, thank you. And you?
— Fine, thank you. See you soon.

blocos.titulo: Un día de Pablo / A day in Pablo's life
blocos.ru: Por la mañana, Pablo dice: «Buenos días.» Por la tarde dice: «Buenas tardes.» Por la noche dice: «Buenas noches.» Con su amiga Lucía dice: «¡Hola! ¿Cómo estás?» Con el señor Ruiz dice: «¿Cómo está usted?» Pablo siempre dice «por favor» y «gracias». Es un chico muy educado.
blocos.pt: In the morning, Pablo says: «Good morning.» In the afternoon he says: «Good afternoon.» At night he says: «Good night.» With his friend Lucía he says: «Hi! How are you?» With Mr. Ruiz he says: «How are you, sir?» Pablo always says «please» and «thank you». He's a very polite young man.

perguntas.pergunta: [misto] What greeting does Pablo use in the afternoon?
[misto] With whom does Pablo use «¿Cómo está usted?», and why?
perguntas.resposta: [misto] With Mr. Ruiz, because it's a formal situation (usted).

perguntas.pergunta: [misto] Which two polite words does Pablo always say?

blocos.enunciado: Play both parts of the dialogue out loud. First with a stranger: «Buenas tardes. ¿Cómo está usted? — Muy bien, gracias. ¿Y usted?» Then with a friend: «¡Hola! ¿Cómo estás? — Bien, gracias. ¿Y tú?» Keep your vowels full and say «Hasta luego» at the end.
